definition.text: Payments offered to farmers or landowners in return for managing their land so that it provides an ecological service.

facts.text: One definition calls PES a transparent system for the additional provision of environmental services through conditional payments to voluntary providers.
The 'big three' services drawing most money are climate change mitigation, watershed services and biodiversity conservation.
The provider usually holds property rights over the land, and receives compensation from those who benefit from its services.
Beneficiaries should pay less than their welfare gain, and providers should accept more than their cost of supplying the service.
Most PES programmes are funded by governments and run through intermediaries such as NGOs, rather than direct buyer-seller contracts.
PES is promoted as a rural development tool, though programmes are usually not designed mainly to reduce poverty.
National set-aside style PES programmes exist in Canada, the EU, Japan and Switzerland as well as the US and China.

title: Theoretical perspectives on PES

definition.text: The three main ways of viewing PES: environmental economics, ecological economics, and the rejection of ecosystem services altogether.

facts.text: Environmental economics sees PES as a voluntary, conditional deal between a service buyer and seller, rooted in the Coase theorem.
In reality transaction costs are almost always present, future payment promises are not time consistent, and financing often runs short.
Ecological economics treats natural and manufactured capital as complements, and judges PES by the weight of the incentive, how direct the transfer is, and how far the service is commodified.
Some services, such as tons of carbon stored, are easy to measure; others are hard.
Critics argue nature should be valued for its own sake and that market framing protects nature only when it is useful to people.
Pragmatists accept the problems of valuing nature but argue that in a commodified society 'something is better than nothing'.

contested_note: Environmental and ecological economists disagree on how to frame PES, and some reject valuing ecosystem services at all.

definition.text: Costa Rica's Pagos por servicios ambientales, set up in 1997 as the first PES programme run on a national scale.

facts.text: It pays for four services: greenhouse gas mitigation, water services, biodiversity protection and scenic beauty.
It was funded at first partly by a fuel tax, with a water tariff added in 2006.
By the end of 2005 its contracts covered 10% of the country, and it is estimated to have prevented 11 million tons of carbon emissions from 1999 to 2005.
Its flat-rate payment leaves many high-value areas unenrolled because their opportunity costs are higher than the payment.

definition.text: A negotiated deal in which the Vittel mineral-water brand paid nearby farmers to adopt practices that protect its groundwater.

facts.text: Intensifying farming from the 1970s raised nitrate levels in the aquifer, threatening the brand.
The pollution came from many diffuse sources, so no single farmer's share could be measured.
The company bought some land and gave technical support and time-limited payments, making it perhaps the world's best-known PES built on direct negotiation.
It is seen as a case of Coasean bargaining, though community grievances and possible overuse of water remain controversial.

title: Hoima and Kibaale PES trial
article: Payment for ecosystem services#Hoima and Kibaale, Uganda

definition.text: A 2010 to 2013 PES scheme in Uganda that was the first set up as a randomized controlled trial to measure its effect on deforestation.

facts.text: Forest owners were paid $28 per hectare per year for two years for keeping forest intact, about 5% of typical annual income.
Deforestation was 2 to 5% in participating villages against 7 to 10% in control villages.
The scheme ended after the evaluation, and old forest practices are assumed to resume once payments stop.

definition.text: A US Department of Agriculture programme that pays farmers to take cropland out of production and plant protective cover such as grass, trees or buffer strips.

facts.text: Its aims are to reduce erosion, improve water quality and benefit wildlife.
It grew out of the 1950s Soil Bank and was formally set up by the 1985 Farm Bill with 10 to 15 year contracts.
Payments are rental payments, cost-share of up to 50% of establishing cover, and extra incentives.
Money limits enrolment, so only the most qualified land receives payments.
By December 1, 2015, it had prevented more than 9 billion tons of soil from eroding.
In 2007 it was estimated to have kept 278 million pounds of nitrogen and 59 million pounds of phosphorus from leaving fields.
Ducks in the Prairie Pothole Region rose 30 percent after 1992 with its help.

definition.text: A mechanism that gives landowners and land managers incentives to look after the environment.

facts.text: England runs such schemes under Environmental Stewardship, administered by Natural England.
After leaving the EU's Common Agricultural Policy, the British government started its Environmental Land Management scheme in 2024.
Since 1998 Switzerland has tied farm subsidies to good environmental practice, such as keeping at least 7% of farmland as ecological compensation areas.

definition.text: A Chinese programme launched in 1999 that pays farmers to convert erosion-prone farmland back to vegetation to curb flooding and soil erosion.

facts.text: It is an example of payment for ecosystem services, offering farmers grain for not farming forested slopes.
It cost $43 billion by one account, with some sources citing $95 billion for the whole programme.
It has involved 124 million people in 1,897 counties in 25 provinces.
By 2010 around 15 million hectares of farmland and 17 million hectares of barren land had returned to natural vegetation.
It has generally been economically positive and has reduced erosion and flooding.
Many plantings were cheap monocultures that did little for biodiversity, though mixed forests could help at little extra cost.

definition.text: Whether an intervention, such as a payment or credit, actually causes an outcome that would not have happened anyway, judged against a baseline.

facts.text: A baseline is a prediction of what the actors would do without the policy, holding everything else constant.
It can be checked after the fact, as in programme evaluation, or beforehand, as an eligibility screen for issuing environmental credits.
Additionality is the impact of the intervention minus the impact of a reference case, net of deadweight, leakage, displacement and substitution.
A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead anyway, for example because it is profitable without carbon credits; that scenario is called business as usual.
Biodiversity offsets must show additionality to compensate for losses, and large offset markets have shown serious shortcomings on it.
The Integrity Council for the Voluntary Carbon Market cited additionality concerns in excluding several renewable energy crediting methods.
Problems with additionality and double counting can undermine the credibility of carbon offsets.
A project is not additional if it would have gone ahead without the credit revenue, for instance because it was profitable anyway.

title: Watershed management

definition.text: The planning and running of programmes that sustain a watershed's functions and share its resources sustainably among its plant, animal and human communities.

facts.text: It covers water supply, water quality, drainage, stormwater runoff and water rights.
On farms it uses buffer strips, grassed waterways, restored wetlands and practices such as conservation tillage and crop rotation.
In towns, retention ponds, filters and wetlands let stormwater soak in so soil and plants filter it before it reaches streams.
Donors backed by the World Bank argue freshwater should be governed as an economic good through pricing, while NGOs see it as a social good.
Groups sharing a watershed often have unequal, divergent interests, so one group's actions can harm others downstream.
Network governance, in which stakeholders form voluntary partnerships, has been adopted by states sharing the Rhine, Nile and Lake Chad basins.

contested_note: Donor institutions and NGOs disagree over whether freshwater should be managed as an economic good or a social good.

title: Conditional cash transfer

definition.text: Programmes that fight poverty by paying cash only to people who meet conditions, such as sending children to school or getting vaccinations.

facts.text: Few development programmes have been evaluated as rigorously.
By 2011 they had spread to 18 Latin American countries, covering up to 129 million people.
Brazil's Bolsa Família pays poor households if school-age children are enrolled and younger children vaccinated.
Evidence from Mexico and Malawi found conditions raised school enrolment compared with unconditional payments.

notes: Seeded in the PES chapter as a model of conditional payments; the dossier has no sentence linking it directly to PES.

title: New York City water supply system
article: New York City water supply system

definition.text: The network of reservoirs, aqueducts and tunnels that supplies New York City with fresh water, kept clean largely by protecting its upstate watersheds.

facts.text: Its three systems, Croton, Catskill and Delaware, reach up to 125 miles (201 km) north of the city.
Since 1997 the city has bought or protected through conservation easements over 130,000 acres (53,000 ha) of watershed land.
Because its watersheds are protected, the system is partly exempt from filtration rules, avoiding more than $10 billion for a filtration plant and at least $100 million a year to run it.
Only 10% of its water is filtered, though all of it is disinfected.
The Department of Environmental Protection runs a $1.5 billion Watershed Protection Program.
It delivers over 1.2 billion US gallons a day to more than eight million city residents.
In 2018 the city announced a US$1 billion investment to keep its unfiltered supply pure, partly against climate-driven turbidity.

definition.text: An auction with one buyer and many sellers, in which sellers compete by underbidding each other.

facts.text: In an ordinary, or forward, auction buyers bid prices up; in a reverse auction prices typically fall.
Government procurement through public tenders is a common example.
Reverse auctions can reveal sellers' private opportunity costs, which helps design incentive programmes for public goods, common-pool resources and ecosystem services.
In a scoring auction, the buyer announces in advance how price and other attributes of each offer will be scored.
A supplier should first work out the lowest price it will accept, which requires knowing its true marginal cost.

definition.text: The rule that a payment for ecosystem services is made only if the service is delivered or the agreed land use is kept up.

facts.text: PES has been defined as additional environmental services secured through conditional payments to voluntary providers.
Design debates focus on how conditionality is set and enforced through monitoring and verification.
Conditional cash transfers for schooling and health use the same idea; in Mexico conditions raised secondary-school attendance most.
Proponents of a rights-based approach to development argue strongly against attaching conditions to social cash transfers.

definition.text: The predicted outcome without a payment or project, against which its real effect is measured.

facts.text: Establishing baselines and counterfactuals is a key challenge for claims that PES is effective.
Under the Clean Development Mechanism, credits are issued for the monitored difference between baseline and actual emissions.
The baseline cannot be observed, so it is built from hypothetical scenarios, similar activities elsewhere, or emissions before the project.
Project partners may gain from a high baseline, risking spurious credits, and offsets can even reward emitting more to inflate the baseline.
How much leakage is counted depends partly on how the baseline is defined.

definition.text: Directing conservation payments to the places where they buy the most environmental benefit for the money.

facts.text: Costa Rica's flat-rate payments leave many high-value areas unenrolled because landowners there face higher opportunity costs.
Its watershed-bound water tariff was criticised for concentrating money in areas of relatively low ecological importance.
Reverse auctions can reveal landowners' private opportunity costs, helping design payment programmes.
With limited money, the Conservation Reserve Program admits only the most qualified land.

definition.text: Payments made only for measured, verified environmental results, such as emission reductions, rather than for planned actions.

facts.text: Most PES programmes pay for management practices and only less commonly for measured outcomes.
REDD+ uses results-based payments to put a financial value on carbon stored in forests, as the last of four stages after readiness, a finance agreement and verification.
The Forest Carbon Partnership Facility's Carbon Fund pays only after independent verification of reported emission reductions.
Countries seeking REDD+ results-based payments must report how the Cancún safeguards are respected and have an assessed forest reference level.
The Green Climate Fund ran a REDD+ results-based payments pilot from 2017 to 2022 and made it a permanent window in 2024.
In farming, the European Commission defines results-based schemes as paying for outcomes such as breeding birds, leaving the methods to the farmer.
REDD+ aims to give financial value to forest carbon through results-based payments.
Payments need a national forest monitoring system, documented methods and data, and reporting under the Warsaw Framework on REDD-plus.
